answer_text:
Let

\[
R_n(x)=f^n(x).
\]

For a rational function, the minimal possible degree of the denominator among all representations as a quotient of polynomials is the degree of the denominator when the rational function is written in lowest terms.

So write

\[
R_n(x)=\frac{P_n(x)}{Q_n(x)}
\]

with \(\gcd(P_n,Q_n)=1\). Then the desired minimal denominator degree is

\[
d_n=\deg Q_n.
\]

Now compute the degrees recursively.

For \(n=1\),

\[
f(x)=x-\frac1x=\frac{x^2-1}{x},
\]

so

\[
P_1(x)=x^2-1,\qquad Q_1(x)=x.
\]

Thus

\[
\deg P_1=2,\qquad \deg Q_1=1.
\]

Assume for some \(n\ge 1\) that

\[
\deg P_n=2^n,\qquad \deg Q_n=2^n-1,
\]

and \(\gcd(P_n,Q_n)=1\). Then

\[
f^{n+1}(x)=f(f^n(x))
=R_n(x)-\frac1{R_n(x)}
=\frac{P_n}{Q_n}-\frac{Q_n}{P_n}
=\frac{P_n^2-Q_n^2}{P_nQ_n}.
\]

Because \(\gcd(P_n,Q_n)=1\), any common factor of \(P_n^2-Q_n^2\) and \(P_nQ_n\) would have to divide both \(P_n\) and \(Q_n\), which is impossible. Hence

\[
P_{n+1}=P_n^2-Q_n^2,\qquad Q_{n+1}=P_nQ_n
\]

is already in lowest terms.

Therefore

\[
\deg Q_{n+1}=\deg P_n+\deg Q_n.
\]

Also, since \(\deg P_n>\deg Q_n\), the leading term of \(P_n^2\) is not canceled by \(Q_n^2\), so

\[
\deg P_{n+1}=2\deg P_n.
\]

Using \(\deg P_1=2\) and \(\deg Q_1=1\), induction gives

\[
\deg P_n=2^n,\qquad \deg Q_n=2^n-1.
\]

Thus the minimal possible denominator degree is

\[
d_n=2^n-1.
\]

\[
\boxed{d_n=2^n-1}
\]
